title: Levodopa-Carbidopa: Timing, Mobility, and Dyskinesia
clientNeeds: Physiological Integrity: Basic Care and Comfort
bottomLine: Levodopa-carbidopa improves Parkinson motor symptoms but does not cure the disease. Consistent dose timing matters because delayed or omitted doses can cause severe immobility, while chronic therapy can produce wearing-off, dyskinesias, hallucinations, and orthostatic hypotension.
recognize: Improved rigidity/bradykinesia supports mobility, swallowing, and ADLs.
Wearing-off occurs when symptoms recur before the next dose; dyskinesias are involuntary movements that can reflect peak dopaminergic effect.
priorities: Administer on the prescribed schedule rather than grouping doses for convenience.
Assess mobility, swallowing, orthostasis, hallucinations, and motor fluctuations.
Use fall precautions and coordinate medication timing with mobility/therapy when possible.
assessMonitor: Trend gait, rigidity, tremor, dyskinesia, hallucinations, BP with position change, swallowing, nausea, and response relative to dose timing.
interventions: Provide assistance during off periods and allow extra time for movement.
If protein significantly interferes with absorption for a specific patient, follow the individualized diet/medication plan rather than broadly restricting protein.
medicationSafety: Abrupt withdrawal or major dose reduction can cause severe rigidity, fever, autonomic instability, and altered mental status resembling NMS.
Dopaminergic drugs may cause impulse-control problems or hallucinations.
redFlags: Fever with severe rigidity after abrupt withdrawal
teaching: Take doses at consistent times and do not stop abruptly; report new hallucinations, severe dizziness, or uncontrolled movements.
delegationScope: Medication timing and effect observation may involve the care team, but new neurologic or psychiatric changes require licensed-nurse assessment.
examTrap: Delaying a scheduled Parkinson medication until after routine care even though the patient depends on dose timing for mobility and swallowing.
oneLinePearl: Parkinson medication timing is functional care, not just pill timing.

title: Valproate: Liver, Platelets, Pregnancy, Ammonia
clientNeeds: Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
bottomLine: Valproate is used for seizure and selected mood/migraine indications but carries serious hepatic, pancreatic, hematologic, hyperammonemic, and fetal risks. New abdominal pain/vomiting, jaundice, unusual bleeding, profound lethargy, or mental-status change requires prompt evaluation.
recognize: Hyperammonemia can cause unexplained lethargy, vomiting, cognitive slowing, or encephalopathy even when liver tests are not dramatically abnormal.
Thrombocytopenia can increase bruising or bleeding.
priorities: Review pregnancy status/potential and indication before therapy because fetal risk is substantial.
Assess liver/pancreatic symptoms, bleeding, and new confusion.
Do not stop antiseizure therapy abruptly unless emergency management directs it.
assessMonitor: Trend liver tests, CBC/platelets, serum valproate when ordered, ammonia when clinically indicated, weight/metabolic effects, and seizure/mood response.
interventions: Use bleeding precautions when thrombocytopenia is significant and reinforce pregnancy-prevention counseling from the prescribing team when applicable.
medicationSafety: Valproate has boxed warnings for hepatotoxicity, fetal risk, and pancreatitis.
Drug interactions can alter valproate or interacting antiseizure-drug concentrations.
teaching: Report abdominal pain, jaundice, severe vomiting, unusual bleeding, or new confusion and discuss pregnancy planning before conception.
delegationScope: Interpretation of toxicity labs and pregnancy-risk decisions require authorized clinician review.
examTrap: Reassuring a profoundly lethargic patient on valproate because the routine liver panel is not severely abnormal without considering hyperammonemia.
oneLinePearl: Valproate toxicity can hit liver, pancreas, platelets, brain, and fetus.

title: Carbamazepine: Blood Counts, Sodium, and Rash
clientNeeds: Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
bottomLine: Carbamazepine treats selected seizure and neuralgia disorders but can cause serious cutaneous reactions, bone-marrow suppression, hyponatremia, hepatic injury, and many drug interactions. Fever/sore throat, rash with mucosal lesions, severe weakness/confusion, or unusual bleeding requires urgent evaluation.
recognize: Hyponatremia may present with headache, confusion, weakness, falls, or seizure.
Agranulocytosis/aplastic anemia can present with infection, pallor, fatigue, or bleeding.
priorities: Assess for rash, infection, bruising/bleeding, and neurologic symptoms.
Review CBC, sodium, liver function, and interacting medications when ordered.
Escalate serious rash or blood-dyscrasia symptoms promptly.
assessMonitor: Trend CBC, sodium, liver tests, serum concentration when indicated, seizure control, gait, vision, and skin/mucosa.
interventions: Use seizure/fall precautions when symptomatic and reinforce lab follow-up.
medicationSafety: Carbamazepine is a strong enzyme inducer that can reduce effectiveness of many medications including hormonal contraceptives.
Certain ancestry/genetic-risk groups may require HLA testing before initiation according to labeling and clinician judgment.
redFlags: Severe confusion or seizure from hyponatremia
teaching: Report rash, mouth sores, fever, sore throat, bruising, or severe weakness immediately and do not stop abruptly without instruction.
delegationScope: Toxicity recognition and laboratory interpretation require licensed-nurse/provider coordination.
examTrap: Treating a new blistering rash as a minor side effect and continuing carbamazepine without urgent evaluation.
oneLinePearl: Carbamazepine: rash, CBC, sodium, liver, interactions.

title: Gabapentin: Sedation, Falls, and Respiratory Risk
clientNeeds: Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
bottomLine: Gabapentin is renally eliminated and can cause dizziness, ataxia, somnolence, and respiratory depression risk when combined with opioids or other CNS depressants, especially in older adults or patients with respiratory disease. Dose adjustment may be needed in renal impairment.
recognize: New gait instability, falls, sedation, confusion, or slowed breathing may represent drug effect or accumulation.
Abrupt withdrawal after regular use can worsen seizures and cause withdrawal symptoms in some patients.
priorities: Assess sedation, respiratory status, gait/fall risk, renal function, and concurrent CNS depressants.
Use extra caution after dose increases or addition of opioids.
Do not stop suddenly when used for seizure control.
assessMonitor: Trend level of consciousness, respiratory rate, falls, edema, renal function, pain/seizure response, and adherence.
interventions: Implement fall precautions and nighttime safety when sedation is present.
medicationSafety: Opioids, benzodiazepines, alcohol, and other sedatives can increase CNS/respiratory depression.
Renal impairment can increase gabapentin exposure.
teaching: Avoid alcohol/other sedatives unless approved and do not drive until the effect is known; report excessive sleepiness or breathing difficulty.
delegationScope: Routine observation may be delegated, but oversedation or respiratory change requires immediate licensed-nurse assessment.
examTrap: Giving scheduled gabapentin and an opioid to an excessively somnolent patient without first assessing respiratory status.
oneLinePearl: Gabapentin + opioids can turn dizziness into respiratory danger.

title: Metronidazole: GI, Neurologic, and Interaction Safety
bottomLine: Metronidazole treats selected anaerobic and protozoal infections. GI upset and metallic taste are common, while new peripheral neuropathy, ataxia, seizure, or encephalopathy during prolonged/high exposure requires prompt evaluation; medication reconciliation is important because major interactions can occur.
recognize: Nausea, abdominal discomfort, and metallic taste are common adverse effects.
Neurologic toxicity can include numbness/tingling, unsteady gait, confusion, or seizure.
priorities: Verify indication and duration and assess baseline neurologic symptoms when prolonged therapy is expected.
Review warfarin and other interacting medications.
Escalate new neurologic symptoms promptly.
assessMonitor: Trend GI tolerance, neurologic symptoms, liver function when indicated, adherence, and INR more closely when used with warfarin under the anticoagulation plan.
interventions: Administer with food when permitted if GI upset occurs and formulation instructions allow.
medicationSafety: Metronidazole can potentiate warfarin anticoagulation.
Alcohol interaction warnings differ across products and evidence; follow current product labeling and prescriber instructions rather than relying on folklore alone.
redFlags: Major bleeding in a patient also taking warfarin
teaching: Complete the prescribed course and report numbness, tingling, severe dizziness, or confusion; check before using alcohol based on the actual product instructions.
delegationScope: New neurologic changes or significant interactions require licensed-nurse/provider review.
examTrap: Ignoring new numbness and gait instability during a prolonged metronidazole course.
oneLinePearl: Metronidazole is more than GI upset—watch nerves and interactions.

title: TMP-SMX: Rash, Potassium, Kidneys, and Blood Counts
clientNeeds: Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
bottomLine: Trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole can cause serious sulfonamide skin reactions, hyperkalemia, renal effects, cytopenias, and important drug interactions. Rash with mucosal involvement, severe weakness/arrhythmia symptoms, marked renal decline, or unusual bleeding requires prompt evaluation.
recognize: Hyperkalemia risk is higher with renal impairment and other potassium-raising drugs.
Bone-marrow effects may present with infection, fatigue, pallor, or bleeding.
priorities: Assess allergy history, renal function, potassium risk, and interacting medications.
Escalate blistering rash, mouth sores, fever with cytopenia concern, or severe hyperkalemia symptoms.
assessMonitor: Trend renal function, potassium, CBC when prolonged/high-risk therapy is used, hydration, rash, and treatment response.
interventions: Maintain appropriate hydration unless contraindicated and reinforce sun protection because photosensitivity can occur.
medicationSafety: Interactions can increase warfarin effect and potassium when combined with ACE inhibitors/ARBs or potassium-sparing agents.
Avoid use in selected pregnancy/neonatal situations according to clinician guidance because folate and bilirubin-related risks matter.
teaching: Report rash, mouth sores, fever, unusual bruising, or severe weakness and use sun protection.
delegationScope: Abnormal potassium, CBC, renal findings, or serious rash require licensed-nurse/provider escalation.
examTrap: Treating a blistering sulfonamide rash as an expected minor allergy symptom.
oneLinePearl: TMP-SMX: skin, potassium, kidneys, blood counts, interactions.

title: Nitrofurantoin: Lower UTI Drug, Not Pyelonephritis Therapy
clientNeeds: Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
bottomLine: Nitrofurantoin is used for selected lower urinary-tract infections because it concentrates in urine; it is not appropriate therapy for pyelonephritis or systemic infection. Renal function, pulmonary/hepatic toxicity symptoms, and peripheral neuropathy matter with prolonged or susceptible-patient use.
recognize: Fever, flank pain, vomiting, hypotension, or systemic illness suggests upper-tract disease rather than uncomplicated cystitis.
Rare pulmonary toxicity can present with cough, dyspnea, fever, or infiltrates.
priorities: Confirm the clinical picture is consistent with lower UTI and assess renal function per product/clinical guidance.
Escalate flank pain/fever/systemic illness instead of assuming treatment failure of simple cystitis.
Report new respiratory, hepatic, or neuropathic symptoms.
assessMonitor: Trend urinary symptoms, fever/flank pain, renal function, respiratory symptoms, liver symptoms, and neuropathy with prolonged exposure.
interventions: Administer with food when product instructions recommend it to improve absorption/tolerance.
medicationSafety: Inadequate renal function can reduce urinary effectiveness and increase toxicity risk.
Long-term prophylactic use requires monitoring for pulmonary/hepatic complications.
teaching: Complete therapy and seek reassessment for fever, flank pain, vomiting, or worsening systemic symptoms.
delegationScope: Recognition of progression from lower UTI to systemic/upper-tract illness requires licensed-nurse assessment.
examTrap: Continuing nitrofurantoin as if it treats pyelonephritis when the patient develops fever and flank pain.
oneLinePearl: Nitrofurantoin belongs in the bladder—not the kidney or bloodstream.

title: Ondansetron: QT and Serotonergic Awareness
clientNeeds: Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
bottomLine: Ondansetron is a 5-HT3 antagonist used for nausea/vomiting. QT prolongation risk is greater in patients with congenital long-QT syndrome, electrolyte abnormalities, bradyarrhythmias, heart failure, or other QT-prolonging drugs; serotonin syndrome is uncommon but possible with serotonergic combinations.
recognize: Headache and constipation are common adverse effects.
Palpitations, syncope, or new dysrhythmia after administration requires prompt evaluation.
priorities: Assess QT-risk factors and potassium/magnesium abnormalities when clinically relevant.
Monitor high-risk patients according to orders.
Escalate syncope, sustained dysrhythmia, or serotonin-syndrome features.
assessMonitor: Trend nausea response, bowel function, rhythm symptoms, electrolytes in high-risk patients, and serotonergic medication combinations.
interventions: Correct electrolyte abnormalities when ordered and use nonpharmacologic nausea measures as appropriate.
medicationSafety: Avoid use in congenital long-QT syndrome according to labeling.
Apomorphine is contraindicated with ondansetron because profound hypotension/loss of consciousness can occur.
complications: Severe constipation/ileus contribution in susceptible patients
teaching: Report fainting, racing/irregular heartbeat, or severe agitation/tremor with fever.
delegationScope: New rhythm or serotonin-toxicity findings require licensed-nurse assessment.
examTrap: Giving repeated ondansetron to a patient with severe hypokalemia and a prolonged QT without addressing the risk.
oneLinePearl: Ondansetron controls nausea; check the QT-risk context in vulnerable patients.

title: Metoclopramide: Tardive Dyskinesia and EPS
clientNeeds: Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
bottomLine: Metoclopramide increases upper-GI motility and is used for selected gastroparesis and refractory GERD situations, but cumulative exposure increases the risk of tardive dyskinesia, which may be irreversible. New involuntary facial/tongue/limb movements or other extrapyramidal symptoms require prompt evaluation and discontinuation according to the prescribing plan.
recognize: Acute dystonia, akathisia, parkinsonism, and tardive dyskinesia are dopamine-blockade adverse effects.
Older adults and prolonged exposure increase TD concern.
priorities: Assess for abnormal involuntary movements before and during ongoing therapy.
Use the shortest effective duration and avoid prolonged routine use beyond labeling limits unless a specialist determines benefit outweighs risk.
Escalate new dyskinesia, rigidity, fever, or severe restlessness.
assessMonitor: Trend abnormal movements, sedation, restlessness, mood changes, renal function, and GI symptom response.
interventions: Use fall precautions when dizziness/sedation occurs and adjust renal dosing through the authorized treatment plan.
medicationSafety: Metoclopramide carries a boxed warning for tardive dyskinesia; 2026 labeling emphasizes shortest-duration use and reassessment.
Antipsychotics and other dopamine antagonists can increase extrapyramidal risk.
teaching: Report lip smacking, tongue movements, facial grimacing, tremor, stiffness, or severe restlessness immediately.
delegationScope: Assessment of new movement disorders and continuation decisions require licensed-nurse/provider escalation.
examTrap: Treating new lip smacking and tongue movements as anxiety and continuing long-term metoclopramide unchanged.
oneLinePearl: Metoclopramide moves the stomach but can create persistent abnormal movements.

title: Lactulose: Bowel Effect and Hepatic Encephalopathy
clientNeeds: Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
bottomLine: Lactulose is an osmotic laxative and is also used to reduce intestinal ammonia absorption in hepatic encephalopathy. For encephalopathy, effectiveness is judged by mental-status improvement and the prescribed stool target—not by producing uncontrolled diarrhea.
recognize: Expected effects include increased soft stools, gas, and cramping.
Excess diarrhea can cause dehydration, hypernatremia or other electrolyte disturbance, renal injury, and worsening weakness.
priorities: Assess mental status, bowel pattern, hydration, abdominal findings, and the prescribed stool goal.
Administer consistently and document stool frequency/character.
Escalate worsening encephalopathy despite therapy or severe diarrhea/dehydration.
assessMonitor: Trend cognition, stool count, intake/output, weight, sodium/potassium/renal function when indicated, and precipitating causes of encephalopathy.
interventions: Protect skin with frequent stools and maintain hydration according to the care plan.
Identify triggers such as GI bleeding, infection, constipation, sedatives, dehydration, or electrolyte disturbance.
medicationSafety: Overtreatment can cause clinically important fluid/electrolyte loss.
Do not automatically hold lactulose after one or two soft stools without checking the ordered target and neurologic status.
teaching: For hepatic encephalopathy, the goal is the prescribed number of soft stools plus clearer thinking—not severe diarrhea.
delegationScope: Stool counts may be delegated with exact reporting parameters; mental-status interpretation and dose-plan changes require licensed clinician review.
examTrap: Holding lactulose simply because the patient has had soft stools even though the encephalopathy treatment target has not been reached.
oneLinePearl: Lactulose for encephalopathy: enough stool to clear ammonia, not enough to dehydrate.
